name: AI adoption
question: Who uses AI, how intensively and for which activities, and how do adoption estimates change with population, questionnaire and organizational context?
synthesis: Across this selected corpus, AI use has expanded in several worker and business surveys, but uptake is uneven and occasional use is much more common than deep integration. Flat Brazilian enterprise estimates, modest shares of AI-assisted work hours and early Danish null earnings and hours effects qualify any simple story of uniform diffusion or immediate transformation. Differences in definitions, sampling frames, weights and questionnaire versions prevent treating the reported percentages as one comparable global adoption rate.

facets.label: Worker and household use
facets.description: Whether people use AI for work, learning or personal purposes, with explicit age, employment and reference-period denominators.

facets.label: Enterprise diffusion
facets.description: Business adoption across size, industry and country, distinguishing enterprise counts from employment-weighted exposure.

facets.label: Frequency and depth of use
facets.description: Days, hours, spending, task breadth, retention and the difference between experimentation and sustained integration.

facets.label: Unequal uptake and access
facets.description: Variation by gender, age, education, occupation, income, geography and business size, without assuming observed gaps are causal.

facets.label: Work organization and outcomes
facets.description: Training, employer policy, functions, tasks and links between adoption, work redesign and measured outcomes.

facets.label: Comparable adoption measures
facets.description: Definitions, question order, reference windows, survey frames, weights, revisions and validation of survey or platform measures.

sources.title: Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users
sources.authors: Adam Grundy, Cory Breaux, Dhanapati Khatiwoda
sources.design: Biweekly weighted Business Trends and Outlook Survey estimates; this official analysis covers the post-questionnaire-change series.
sources.population: U.S. employer businesses in the BTOS nonfarm scope; firm-weighted rates, not the share of workers using AI.
sources.duration: December 14, 2025-May 3, 2026 observations summarized in a May 26, 2026 release.
sources.measure: AI use in any business function during the prior two weeks; separate expected use in the next six months.
sources.finding: Recent use ranged from 17% to 20% over the reviewed window; expected use ranged from 20% to 23%. Increases were evident for businesses with at least 20 employees but not statistically significant for smaller firms.
sources.limitations: The November 2025 wording change breaks comparability with the earlier production-only series. Intentions are not realized adoption; this release does not establish task intensity.
sources.locator: Opening results; How BTOS Measures AI Use; firm-size comparisons.
sources.sourceNote: Read the official May 26 article and the separate wording notice. This is a dated analytical release, not a claim that May is the latest available BTOS observation.
sources.selectionReason: A national official recurring firm measure with an explicit questionnaire break and useful size heterogeneity.
sources.headline: Firm adoption varies by size, and the late-2025 series starts a new comparison baseline.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing BTOS seed -> Census 2026 AI-use business article -> official question-wording notice.

sources.title: AI Question Wording Updates
sources.design: Official instrument revision and comparability notice, supported by cognitive-testing observations; not a new prevalence estimate.
sources.population: BTOS business respondents.
sources.duration: Revision implemented November 17, 2025; notice December 3, 2025; new-series release December 4.
sources.measure: Scope of business AI questions, retaining the two-week recent-use window.
sources.finding: The question changed from producing goods or services to any business function. Cognitive testing found respondents could omit administrative or other uses under the old wording; Census treats the revised estimates as a new series.
sources.limitations: The notice does not identify a randomized bridge estimate separating real diffusion from wording effects.
sources.locator: Four-page notice: revised wording and new time-series guidance.
sources.sourceNote: Read the complete notice. Framework/none denotes instrument guidance, not a longitudinal study or an independently measured adoption wave.
sources.searchOrigin: Census BTOS article -> official AI Question Wording Updates PDF.

sources.title: Tracking Firm Use of AI in Real Time: A Snapshot from the Business Trends and Outlook Survey
sources.authors: Kathryn Bonney, Cory Breaux, Catherine Buffington, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster, Nathan Goldschlag, John Haltiwanger, Zachary Kroff, Keith Savage
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau, CES Working Paper 24-16
sources.design: Foundational analysis of successive BTOS cross-sections and the first AI supplement.
sources.population: U.S. employer businesses in the BTOS frame.
sources.duration: September 2023-February 2024; March 2024 working-paper landing-page abstract.
sources.measure: AI used to produce goods or services; anticipated adoption, business characteristics and reported adjustments.
sources.finding: Biweekly firm adoption rose from 3.7% to 5.4% over the reported period. Few adopters reported AI-related employment reductions; uptake differed by firm age, size and sector.
sources.limitations: Older, narrower wording. The projected 6.6% rate for early fall 2024 is an expectation, not an observed outcome. Abstract inspection cannot assess all robustness checks.
sources.locator: Official landing-page Abstract.
sources.sourceNote: Official abstract inspected; NBER version was inaccessible. Do not merge its earlier estimates mechanically with the revised 2025-26 series or count the BTOS family as independent surveys.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Census/Bonney seed -> NBER access failure -> Census CES-WP-24-16 primary abstract.

sources.title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
sources.authors: Kathryn Bonney, Cory Breaux, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster, John Haltiwanger, Aditya Pande
sources.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau, CES Working Paper 26-25
sources.design: Pooled second BTOS AI supplement with weighted function/task measures and conditional regressions.
sources.population: U.S. employer firms; worker use is reported by the business, not independently surveyed employees.
sources.duration: Collected November 17, 2025-February 8, 2026 across six biweekly panels; April 2026 paper.
sources.measure: Formal firm adoption, AI use across business functions, worker-task use and organizational changes.
sources.finding: Formal adoption was approximately 18% of firms, while reported worker-task use occurred at 23% of firms. Corresponding employment-weighted rates were 32% and 41%; these mean employment at adopting firms, not individual workers' use rates.
sources.limitations: Pooled cross-section, not a followed-firm adoption panel. Employer awareness and interpretation matter; regressions do not identify causal productivity or employment effects.
sources.locator: Section 2.1-2.2; Section 4 overlap analysis; Section 9 survey comparison; Section 10.
sources.sourceNote: Read methods, overlap results, comparison discussion and conclusion in the 79-page PDF, not every appendix calculation. Collection dates differ from reference periods; sample-frame size is not completed interviews.
sources.searchOrigin: Search Census AI adoption 2026 -> CES-WP-26-25 official PDF.

sources.title: The State of Generative AI Adoption in 2025
sources.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.design: Authors' report on quarterly nationally representative online Real-Time Population Survey estimates and a question-order correction.
sources.population: U.S. adults aged 18-64; work-use and work-hours measures use the employed population.
sources.duration: August 2024-August 2025; released November 13, 2025.
sources.measure: Self-reported generative AI use for work and nonwork; awareness/use question sequence.
sources.finding: Overall use rose from a revised 44.6% in August 2024 to 54.6% in August 2025. The original August 2024 estimate was 39.4%; testing of question sequencing led to reweighting earlier waves.
sources.limitations: Self-reported use is not observed output. Historical-computer comparisons involve different technologies and survey contexts. Self-assessed time savings and modeled productivity are not randomized effects.
sources.locator: Generative AI Adoption Continues to Climb and its methodological footnote; Beyond the Adoption Rate.
sources.sourceNote: Read author summary, revision note and productivity caveats. Full updated paper was not retrieved; do not reuse the unrevised 39.4% as a comparable baseline.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing RPS/Bick seed -> November 2025 St. Louis Fed author update.

sources.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Work Hours Assisted: Employed Adults
sources.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming
sources.publisher: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis; RPS authors
sources.design: Quarterly weighted survey series; assisted-hour bounds are constructed from bracketed days and time answers.
sources.population: Employed U.S. adults aged 18-64; denominator is total work hours, including nonusers.
sources.duration: Quarterly tracker; inspected Q3 2025-Q3 2026 observations, updated October 20, 2026 at 10:50 AM CDT.
sources.measure: Midpoint of lower and upper bounds on generative-AI-assisted work hours; nonusers assigned zero.
sources.finding: The displayed midpoint was 5.31% of total work hours in Q3 2026, versus 6.27% in Q2 and 5.73% in Q3 2025. These point estimates alone do not establish a statistically significant decline.
sources.limitations: Recall, category widths and midpoint assumptions affect estimates. Not seasonally adjusted; no uncertainty interval was exposed on the inspected series page. Assisted hours are not hours eliminated.
sources.locator: Observations table and Notes.
sources.sourceNote: Verified the dated observations and construction notes directly on FRED. Shares rounded to two decimals here. Same RPS family as the adoption and cross-country papers.
sources.selectionReason: Adds a current recurring measure of intensity with a clear hours denominator and explicit construction assumptions.
sources.headline: AI-assisted hours are a much narrower measure than the share of workers who have tried AI.
sources.searchOrigin: RPS public tracker trail -> FRED RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL.

sources.title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy
sources.design: Analytical comparison of BTOS, RPS and Survey of Business Uncertainty measures; no newly fielded adoption survey.
sources.population: Businesses, workers and senior business leaders in different U.S. survey frames.
sources.duration: Evidence through 2025; published April 3, 2026.
sources.measure: Firm-count adoption, individual work use and employment-weighted presence at adopting firms.
sources.finding: Apparently divergent adoption estimates partly measure different populations and concepts. The SBU's high employment-weighted adoption estimate is not the percentage of workers personally using AI.
sources.limitations: Survey contrasts are not an experimental decomposition of all discrepancies. The AI-specific SBU evidence is a November 2025 module, despite the underlying survey's recurring operation.
sources.locator: Opening comparison; survey-specific sections and concluding discussion.
sources.sourceNote: Read full note and methodological caveats. Included as a measurement synthesis, not an independent prevalence observation or a longitudinal series.
sources.searchOrigin: Search official US AI adoption survey comparability -> April 2026 FEDS Notes.

sources.title: U.S. Workers Are More Worried Than Hopeful About Future AI Use in the Workplace
sources.design: Weighted American Trends Panel survey, recruited through national address-based probability sampling, online and telephone.
sources.population: 5,273 employed U.S. adults answering about their main job.
sources.duration: October 7-13, 2024 fieldwork; February 25, 2025 publication.
sources.measure: Amount of work done with AI, chatbot use and workplace expectations.
sources.finding: 16% said at least some of their work was done with AI. Adoption and attitudes varied across worker groups; concern about future effects does not itself measure current use.
sources.limitations: Question wording and broad AI awareness differ from named-tool and ever-use surveys. This analysis is one survey wave, despite recruitment from a panel.
sources.locator: How we did this; opening findings on current use and worker differences.
sources.sourceNote: Read report overview and sampling description; no respondent-level data reanalysis. Publication date must not be mistaken for the October 2024 measurement date.
sources.searchOrigin: Search official worker AI surveys -> Pew February 2025 workplace report.

sources.title: Global Indicator: Artificial Intelligence
sources.design: Recurring employee survey indicator reporting frequency and organizational perceptions.
sources.population: U.S. employees; some organizational-effect questions are restricted to employees in AI-implementing organizations.
sources.duration: Inspected October 22, 2026; quantitative text explicitly refers to May 2026.
sources.measure: Daily, several-times-weekly and several-times-yearly work use; perceived productivity and organizational integration.
sources.finding: For May 2026, 15% reported daily use, 30% use a few times a week or more, and 52% a few times a year or more. These nested frequency thresholds yield very different adoption headlines.
sources.limitations: Indicator page does not expose enough wave-level sample detail for an independent precision assessment. Manager-support associations and self-rated productivity are not causal estimates.
sources.locator: What Percentage of Employees Use AI at Work?; Does AI Improve Productivity at Work?
sources.sourceNote: Read indicator text. Metadata says updated April 2026 while body says May and image label mentions Q3; retain May as the explicit observation period and flag the inconsistency.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Gallup adoption seed -> live AI indicator; industry link returned same indicator.

sources.title: How Gallup Developed Global Survey Questions About AI
sources.design: Qualitative cognitive interviews testing interpretation of draft global survey questions.
sources.population: 48 participants, including AI users and nonusers; not a probability prevalence sample.
sources.geography: Colombia, India, South Africa and United Kingdom
sources.duration: November-December 2025 interviews; June 24, 2026 report.
sources.measure: Interpretation of AI definitions, awareness and frequency categories.
sources.finding: Participants often understood AI primarily as chatbots; abstract definitions confused some respondents. Once-daily and multiple-daily use were meaningfully different, prompting revised frequency categories.
sources.limitations: Small purposive qualitative sample cannot estimate national adoption or guarantee cross-language measurement equivalence. Planned World Poll coverage is not a completed global result.
sources.locator: People Think AI = Generative AI; AI Needs to Be Defined Through Use Cases and Tools; Daily Users Are Not All the Same.
sources.sourceNote: Read the methodological report. Classified as an empirical snapshot because it reports new interviews, rather than treating all questionnaire work as theory.
sources.searchOrigin: Search Gallup AI survey methodology -> June 2026 cognitive-interview report.

sources.title: 20% of EU enterprises use AI technologies
sources.design: Annual harmonized ICT usage and e-commerce enterprise surveys, compiled by national statistical agencies.
sources.population: Enterprises with at least 10 employees or self-employed persons in NACE C-J, L-N and group 95.1.
sources.duration: 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2025 estimates; December 11, 2025 release.
sources.measure: Use of at least one enumerated AI technology; broader than generative AI alone.
sources.finding: 20.0% of in-scope EU enterprises used AI in 2025, compared with 13.5% in 2024. Country differences were substantial, with Denmark at 42.0% and Romania at 5.2%.
sources.limitations: Excludes microenterprises and several sectors. Generation of pictures, videos or sound was newly included in 2025, so technology coverage changed. These are enterprise rates, not worker rates.
sources.locator: Opening findings; country chart; Methodological notes; dataset isoc_eb_ai.
sources.sourceNote: Read official release and methodological notes. No downloaded microdata or country-specific nonresponse assessment; national differences should not be interpreted as causal policy effects.
sources.selectionReason: Official recurring non-U.S. firm evidence with explicit coverage and substantial cross-country variation.
sources.headline: European enterprise adoption rose, but country coverage and technology definitions matter.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Eurostat enterprise seed -> December 2025 official release and methodological notes.

sources.title: 64% of 16-24-year-olds used AI in 2025
sources.design: 2025 household and individual ICT survey comparison by age and purpose.
sources.population: EU people aged 16-74, with a separate 16-24 subgroup; not restricted to employed workers.
sources.duration: 2025 survey, use during the preceding three months; released February 10, 2026.
sources.measure: Generative AI use overall and for private, educational and professional purposes.
sources.finding: Use was reported by 63.8% of people aged 16-24 and 32.7% of those aged 16-74. Professional-purpose use was much closer across these groups than overall use, while education and private use differed more.
sources.limitations: The younger group is contained in the overall comparison group. Professional-use percentages use population denominators, not employed-worker denominators. Only one relevant wave was assessed.
sources.locator: Opening age comparison; purpose-of-use paragraph; Methodological notes.
sources.sourceNote: Read official article including denominator and reference-period notes. An annually recurring parent survey does not by itself make this one-wave AI analysis longitudinal.
sources.searchOrigin: Eurostat enterprise trail -> February 2026 individual generative-AI release.

sources.title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026
sources.design: Weighted Business Insights and Conditions Survey trend analysis with new depth-of-use questions.
sources.population: UK businesses with at least 10 employees in covered sectors; excludes finance/insurance and several public and primary sectors.
sources.duration: September 2023-June 2026; latest included fieldwork June 15-28, 2026, wave 159; published July 20.
sources.measure: Any AI technology use, number of technologies and extent of integration.
sources.finding: Any AI use rose from 12% in September 2023 to about 35% in June 2026 among in-scope businesses with at least 10 employees. Only 10% of AI-using businesses in that size scope reported extensive use.
sources.limitations: Voluntary survey and official statistics in development. Extent questions were newly introduced; the whole trend cannot be read as a stable integration-depth series.
sources.locator: Main points; business adoption trend; extent of use; Data sources and quality.
sources.sourceNote: Read full analytical article and quality section. Recurring survey estimates, not demonstrated follow-up of the same firms. Small-firm and sector exclusions constrain comparisons with BTOS.
sources.searchOrigin: Search ONS AI business 2026 -> official 2023-to-2026 analysis.

sources.title: Characteristics of Australian Business, 2024-25 financial year
sources.design: Recurring business survey publication with ICT checklist and industry/innovation breakdowns.
sources.population: Australian businesses in the publication's scope, including microbusiness size categories; not limited to firms with 10 or more workers.
sources.duration: 2024-25 financial year; released June 25, 2026; historical comparisons displayed for prior surveys.
sources.measure: AI as one item in a multiple-response list of technologies used in the business.
sources.finding: 12% reported AI use in 2024-25; information, media and telecommunications reached 38%, compared with 1% in transport, postal and warehousing.
sources.limitations: The question explicitly does not measure extent or intensity. Historical reference year is inconsistent: key statistics say 2022-23, whereas the ICT section says 2021-22 for the earlier 1% estimate.
sources.locator: Key statistics; Business use of Information and Communication Technology; industry table.
sources.sourceNote: Read release and AI tables, not all survey methodology attachments. Historical growth is not quantified here until the baseline-year discrepancy is resolved; latest-release URL can change.
sources.searchOrigin: Search ABS official AI adoption -> Characteristics of Australian Business latest release.

sources.title: TIC Empresas 2024: Pesquisa sobre o uso das tecnologias de informacao e comunicacao nas empresas brasileiras
sources.publisher: Comite Gestor da Internet no Brasil
sources.design: Stratified random enterprise survey with telephone interviews, weights and repeated published AI indicators.
sources.population: Registered active private enterprises with at least 10 persons occupied in specified CNAE sectors; 4,453 completed interviews in 2024.
sources.duration: March-November 2024 fieldwork; comparisons with 2021 and 2023; released May 13, 2025.
sources.measure: Enterprise AI use, technology types and acquisition arrangements.
sources.finding: 13% of in-scope enterprises reported AI use in 2024, the same rounded share as in 2021 and 2023. Large enterprises and information/communication firms each reported 38%.
sources.limitations: Excludes microenterprises, informal businesses and several sectors. Low response, approximately 9% in the fieldwork table, leaves nonresponse concerns despite weighting. Equal rounded rates do not prove zero underlying change.
sources.locator: Methodological report, printed pp. 29-34; fieldwork report pp. 48-53; AI results and official May 13 release.
sources.sourceNote: Checked population, sampling and response tables in Portuguese PDF plus release at https://cetic.br/pt/noticia/empresas-contratam-solucoes-de-ia-no-setor-privado-mas-parcerias-com-universidades-ainda-sao-limitadas-revela-pesquisa/. Methods clarify 10-or-more despite looser press wording.
sources.selectionReason: Substantive non-European evidence and a flat reported trend that qualifies uniform-growth narratives.
sources.headline: Brazil's reported enterprise AI share stayed flat, with much higher uptake in large firms.
sources.searchOrigin: Search Cetic TIC Empresas 2024 AI -> official release -> PDF without www after first host failed.

sources.title: AI measurement in ICT usage surveys: A review
sources.design: Cross-country review of official statistical AI definitions and ICT business-survey questions.
sources.population: Selected OECD countries' official enterprise measures and complementary nonofficial sources.
sources.duration: Published March 1, 2021; pre-generative-AI-boom measurement landscape.
sources.measure: How survey definitions and questions operationalize AI adoption.
sources.finding: The review catalogs different definitions and instruments, illustrating why an adoption percentage needs its statistical definition and survey scope attached.
sources.limitations: Historical review, not a current diffusion estimate. Full report was unavailable through the inspected download link; detailed recommendations were not assessed.
sources.locator: Official OECD.AI Abstract and publication date.
sources.sourceNote: Official abstract inspected only. Corporate author used because individual author metadata was not established; no claim of full-text assessment.
sources.searchOrigin: Search OECD AI measurement ICT usage surveys -> official 2021 review page; download failed.

sources.title: The unequal adoption of ChatGPT exacerbates existing inequalities among workers
sources.design: Worker adoption survey linked to preexisting administrative registers.
sources.population: 18,000 workers in 11 AI-exposed occupations.
sources.duration: 2023 adoption survey; repository journal-article version dated December 30, 2024.
sources.measure: ChatGPT use at work, worker characteristics, prior earnings and perceived barriers.
sources.finding: Women were 16 percentage points less likely to have used ChatGPT for work in this surveyed population. Users were younger and less experienced yet already earned somewhat more before ChatGPT's arrival.
sources.limitations: Exposed occupations are not the entire labor market. Adoption differences are not causal treatment effects; register linkage to earlier earnings does not establish a longitudinal adoption trajectory.
sources.locator: Repository Description and bibliographic metadata.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected official author-institution abstract; full-text download failed. Wording about training/restrictions is based on the abstract, not independent review of survey instruments.
sources.searchOrigin: Search Humlum Vestergaard ChatGPT unequal adoption -> UChicago repository primary record.

sources.title: Still waters, rapid currents: Early labor market transformation under generative AI
sources.design: Worker surveys linked to monthly administrative worker and workplace outcomes; observational before/after and adopter comparisons.
sources.population: Approximately 25,000 surveyed Danish workers in 11 highly exposed occupations; linked workplace records.
sources.duration: Late-2023 and late-2024 surveys; monthly administrative outcomes through December 2024; author summary October 6, 2026.
sources.measure: Chatbot adoption, employer encouragement/training, work reorganization, earnings, hours and occupational mobility.
sources.finding: Authors report early null average earnings and hours effects, ruling out effects larger than 2% in their design, despite substantial task and employer-policy changes. Occupational mobility differs positively for adopters.
sources.limitations: Short early horizon, selected occupations and observational identification. Null averages do not exclude subgroup effects or later impacts; mobility association is not proof of causation.
sources.locator: Key findings; A clean early window on AI adoption; employer policies and labor-market outcomes.
sources.sourceNote: Read the authors' detailed summary, not inaccessible NBER paper. Longitudinal refers to the same linked units' administrative outcomes; it does not assert every survey respondent answered both waves.
sources.searchOrigin: Humlum/Vestergaard paper trail -> October 2026 author summary of revised NBER 33777.

sources.title: What Work Does Generative AI Do?
sources.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David J. Deming, Tyler Schumacher
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis; Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco EERN
sources.design: Nationally representative worker survey linking reported generative AI use to detailed job tasks.
sources.population: U.S. workers performing surveyed job tasks; detailed sample counts not available in the inspected abstract.
sources.duration: Primary abstract posted July 7, 2026; exact fieldwork period not established from inspected material.
sources.measure: Occupation- and task-specific adoption, compared with exposure scores and platform-inferred tasks.
sources.finding: Adoption is broad but uneven even among workers doing similar work. Survey-derived task shares differ from chat-log classifications, which the authors find overassign generic tasks relative to O*NET.
sources.limitations: Abstract-only inspection; no independent check of weighting, mapping validity or task-level confidence intervals. Exposure remains distinct from actual use.
sources.locator: Author list, posting date and primary abstract.
sources.sourceNote: Read Fed-hosted abstract. NBER access failed; later working-paper versions may differ. Detailed numeric breadth claims withheld without methods inspection.
sources.searchOrigin: Search What Work Does Generative AI Do -> Fed EERN primary abstract after NBER access failure.

sources.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
sources.design: Privacy-preserving automated classification of platform conversations, with comparisons to earlier samples.
sources.population: Claude.ai users and first-party API traffic; geographic analysis samples one million Claude.ai Free, Pro and Max conversations.
sources.geography: Countries with observed Claude use and U.S. states; not a representative global worker sample.
sources.duration: November 13-20, 2025 geographic sample, compared with January/August 2025 releases; January 15, 2026 report.
sources.measure: Task purpose, augmentation/automation, inferred skills, autonomy and geographic usage.
sources.finding: Usage mix and augmentation/automation shares changed across samples. Adoption and task mix differed by geography; conversation-level evidence reveals depth but cannot supply population adoption rates.
sources.limitations: Vendor selection, classifier error and changing users/tools. Inferred task success is not independently verified completion. Productivity extrapolations are model-based, not observed aggregate gains.
sources.locator: Chapters 1 and 3; chapter 3 sample footnote 2; geographic and augmentation analyses.
sources.sourceNote: Inspected report methods, comparisons and geographic analysis; did not reproduce classifications. Safety-flagged conversations were excluded from the geographic sample.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Anthropic Economic Index seed -> January 2026 economic-primitives report.

sources.title: Ramp AI Index
sources.authors: Ramp Economics Lab, Ara Kharazian, Ian Macomber
sources.design: Monthly classification of AI purchases from merchant names and transaction line items among Ramp customers.
sources.population: U.S. businesses on Ramp; current page describes transaction data from more than 85,000 firms.
sources.duration: Monthly series; inspected September 2026 table on October 22, 2026 and April 14, 2025 methodology.
sources.measure: Share of businesses with AI-product spending in the month, not all use or active users.
sources.finding: The current table reports 55.9% of U.S. businesses on Ramp spending on AI in September 2026. Purchase-based measurement can move differently from survey use or hours.
sources.limitations: Customer selection, changing coverage, merchant classifications and revisions. Free tools, personal accounts and some bundled services are missed; payment does not establish productive usage.
sources.locator: Latest data table and metric definition; How we built The Ramp AI Index, methodology.
sources.sourceNote: Read https://ramp.com/data/how-we-built-the-ramp-ai-index and September commentary. Older commentary values differ from current table; use this dated current vintage. No population representativeness or Census reweighting is assumed without documentation.
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Ramp seed -> September 2026 commentary -> live table -> linked original methodology.

sources.title: How People Use ChatGPT
sources.authors: Aaron Chatterji, Tom Cunningham, David Deming, Zoe Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Shan, Kevin Wadman
sources.design: Repeated sampled-message classifications, account-level usage records and an aggregated employment-data linkage.
sources.population: Consumer ChatGPT Free, Plus and Pro users; excludes enterprise, business and education plans.
sources.geography: Global platform users, with available country/demographic classifications.
sources.duration: September 15, 2025 paper; main classified-message sample May 15, 2024-June 26, 2025, with some analyses through July 31.
sources.measure: Work/nonwork message mix and task types; denominators are messages, not workers or work hours.
sources.finding: Estimated nonwork share rose from 53% to 73% of consumer messages in the compared June 2024/2025 seven-day windows, while absolute work-message volume also increased.
sources.limitations: Classified sample excludes opt-outs, minors, logged-out users and unavailable conversations. Automated intent classification is fallible; inferred gender is not self-reported. Use does not prove realized economic value.
sources.locator: Table 1; Sections 3.1-3.2; Appendix B classifier validation.
sources.sourceNote: Checked sample restrictions, dated table and validation discussion in primary PDF. Classification here follows the repeated message-mix outcome; the paper also includes account-cohort analyses.
sources.searchOrigin: Search How People Use ChatGPT -> NBER access failure -> author-hosted OpenAI paper.

sources.title: How ChatGPT adoption has expanded
sources.design: Account-signup cohort follow-up using a 0.1% user sample; additional aggregate regional analyses.
sources.population: Individual-plan accounts created October 15, 2025-May 1, 2026; excludes banned users, minors and accounts with no messages in the initial 28 days.
sources.geography: Supported ChatGPT countries; global platform users.
sources.duration: Account activity through May 31, 2026; June 30 report; up to approximately six months for earliest cohorts.
sources.measure: Messages in the preceding 28 days relative to the first 28; cumulative distinct classifier-defined capabilities.
sources.finding: The report describes higher message volume and broader use six months after signup within eligible account cohorts. This is follow-up of accounts, not population diffusion.
sources.limitations: Eligibility and attrition can bias generalization. Cumulative breadth mechanically increases with opportunities to try categories; commercial provider analysis is not an independent welfare evaluation.
sources.locator: ChatGPT users deepened and expanded their use over time, including sample and exclusion paragraphs.
sources.sourceNote: Read full account-cohort methods summary. Exact handling of inactivity after the initial window is not sufficiently documented for an independent retention reconstruction.
sources.searchOrigin: OpenAI usage-paper trail -> Signals June 30, 2026 account-cohort report.

sources.title: Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.
sources.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming, Nicola Fuchs-Schundeln, Jonas Jessen
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis; author summary of BPEA conference paper
sources.design: Harmonized worker surveys in seven countries across two rounds, supplemented by official enterprise data.
sources.population: Employed workers in nationally representative country surveys; not all adults or every European country.
sources.geography: United States, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Italy, Sweden and Netherlands.
sources.duration: May-June 2025 and January-February 2026 surveys; March 30, 2026 author summary.
sources.measure: Workplace generative AI adoption and active-use hours, using coordinated worker questions.
sources.finding: Early-2026 work adoption was 43.0% in the U.S.; European countries ranged from 36.3% in the U.K. to 25.6% in Italy. Differences in hours were larger than differences in any use.
sources.limitations: Self-reports and country composition remain important. Industry productivity associations are not randomized causal effects; cross-country firm surveys have noncomparable questions.
sources.locator: How Did We Measure AI Adoption?; Finding 1; survey-comparability note.
sources.sourceNote: Read authors' Fed summary. The BPEA draft PDF exceeded the web retrieval limit, so no full-paper review claimed. Two survey rounds do not establish same-worker longitudinal follow-up.
sources.selectionReason: Coordinated cross-country worker measurement helps distinguish real country differences from comparisons of incompatible surveys.
sources.headline: Comparable worker questions show both adoption and intensity gaps across the Atlantic.

sources.title: Adoption and investment in AI across the euro area: Insights from harmonised firm-level data
sources.authors: Annalisa Ferrando, Sara Lamboglia, Judit Rariga, Maurice Schmidt
sources.design: Two ad hoc SAFE modules with different questions; weighted cross-sectional adoption analysis and an embedded information experiment on investment expectations.
sources.population: Nonfinancial manufacturing, construction, trade and service firms; December module reports 5,067 respondents.
sources.duration: June and December 2025 modules; 2026 Occasional Paper 395.
sources.measure: December self-rated AI intensity, including pilots; June past/current investment. Published weights reflect employment/economic significance across strata.
sources.finding: Approximately 70% reported some AI use under this broad weighted definition, but only 7% significant use. This is not directly comparable to Eurostat's enterprise-count rate.
sources.limitations: Different module questions are not a like-for-like adoption trend. Positive productivity/employment associations are observational. The information experiment concerns plans, not realized AI implementation.
sources.locator: Sections 2.1-2.2; Section 3.1 and Chart 1 notes; Section 8 experiment description.
sources.sourceNote: Read methods, questionnaire text, adoption tables and experiment description. Retained snapshot because the reported adoption outcome is December-only; not labeled longitudinal merely because SAFE recurs.
sources.searchOrigin: Search ECB adoption investment AI euro area -> Occasional Paper 395 official PDF.

gaps.title: Bridge definitions before comparing diffusion
gaps.summary: The reviewed rates cannot yet be combined into one reliable ranking or continuous cross-survey adoption trend.
gaps.basis: BTOS changed wording, RPS revised question sequencing, Eurostat expanded technology coverage, and SAFE counts experimental use with different weights. Harmonized worker questions in Mind the Gap improve comparability but do not resolve firm/worker or survey/log differences.
gaps.next: Run randomized bridge questionnaires on common samples, publish old/new definitions in parallel, and report firm-count, employment-weighted, person and hours denominators separately with uncertainty.

gaps.title: Measure sustained intensity, not only trial
gaps.summary: There is limited cross-source calibration of frequency, assisted hours, purchases and observed task activity in this corpus.
gaps.basis: Gallup's thresholds produce sharply different rates; RPS hours are bracket midpoints; Ramp measures payment; platform messages have different user and task mixes. OpenAI's account follow-up adds genuine longitudinal evidence but excludes parts of the population and needs clearer retention handling.
gaps.next: Follow consenting workers and firms with repeated time diaries plus privacy-preserving usage logs, recording inactive periods, task quality, unbundled costs and changes in tool coverage; validate survey categories against those records.

gaps.title: Distinguish barriers from task fit and unequal opportunity
gaps.summary: Observed adoption gaps do not reveal how much comes from access, training, employer restrictions or genuine differences in useful tasks.
gaps.basis: Danish worker gaps, Eurostat age/country differences and business size gradients coexist with Brazil's flat aggregate share. Gallup's qualitative work shows even the meaning of AI use varies. These selected sources do not supply comparable causal barrier estimates across settings.
gaps.next: Evaluate training, access and policy changes using randomized encouragement or credible rollout designs, stratified by worker and firm characteristics, including microenterprises and lower-income settings missing from much of this corpus.

gaps.title: Connect actual adoption to organizational outcomes
gaps.summary: The path from tool use to durable work redesign and economic outcomes remains uncertain in the reviewed evidence.
gaps.basis: Census finds worker-task use can occur without formal firm adoption; ONS distinguishes broad uptake from extensive integration. Danish linked records show early null earnings/hours effects despite organizational changes, while SAFE and self-report studies show positive associations or perceptions that use different outcomes and designs.
gaps.next: Link same-worker and same-firm adoption histories to administrative outcomes and independently assessed output over several years, separating access, use intensity, training, reorganization, selection and changes in task demand.

reviewNotes: This is a bounded, AI-assisted scoping scan, not a systematic review or an exhaustive bibliography. Assessments have not received independent human review. Access-depth status describes the primary material inspected, not its truth or peer-review status.

There are 25 source records but fewer independent evidence families: BTOS, RPS and associated syntheses overlap; linked Danish studies also share a research program. Do not count articles as independent replications.
Highlighted evidence balances official firm diffusion, worker hours, harmonized geography and a flat non-European trend; none of these highlighted sources is a longitudinal causal study.

Temporal classification follows the assessed outcome: repeated estimates need comparable measurement occasions, longitudinal means actual same-unit follow-up, and none covers reviews/instrument guidance without new outcome measurement.

The Denmark outcome record is longitudinal because administrative outcomes follow linked workers/workplaces, not because both survey rounds necessarily contain identical respondents. OpenAI cohort follow-up is longitudinal but platform-selected.

Census wording and reference periods require careful versioning. The November 2025 discontinuity combines instrument changes and elapsed diffusion; it cannot all be credited to new adoption. Core questions and supplements use different reference windows.

RPS historical revisions, bracket midpoint assumptions and current FRED vintages should be carried into any chart. The current hours series is not seasonally adjusted; a point-estimate dip is not proof of a significant reversal.

Eurostat enterprises, SAFE firms, worker surveys and household surveys have different frames and weights. Professional-purpose household use is not employed-worker use; employment at an adopting firm is not personal use.

Brazil's full methodology resolves the release's loose size wording as at least 10 persons occupied. Its low response and sector/microenterprise exclusions deserve explicit treatment before stronger international comparisons.

ABS release has conflicting historical baseline years. Gallup indicator has conflicting update/observation labels and limited wave methods on the indicator page. These ambiguities are preserved rather than silently repaired.

Platform samples omit important use: enterprise versus consumer products, privacy opt-outs, free or personal purchases, unsupported countries and inactive accounts. Message share, paid adoption and user retention should occupy separate measures.

Use, self-reported time savings, output quality, earnings, hours and employment are different outcomes. Positive subjective productivity and early null administrative effects can coexist without contradiction.

Full underlying papers were not obtained for several abstract/summary records. Important follow-up checks include task-survey field dates/sample design, RPS revised questionnaire appendix, Danish identification details and account-cohort attrition handling.

Geographic coverage is uneven within this corpus. Canadian and Singapore official leads were not assessed due access failures; absence from the file is not evidence that those countries lack relevant research.

Search and checks occurred on 2026-10-22. Publication year, fieldwork period, observation vintage and future intentions are separately recorded; this file does not claim that each included release is the latest available anywhere.
